passage:
"So who's leading?" Anjali asked, stirring her coffee in the canteen.
"Joseph, obviously," said Rafiq. "Did you hear his pitch in class? Like a real CEO."
"Exactly," Anjali said. "He talks like someone who runs companies."
Kiran looked up from her laptop. "Last semester, Joseph's group submitted two days late."
"That was probably the group's fault."
"And Hemlata did all their data work. On time."
"Hemlata barely speaks in meetings," Anjali said. "Leaders need to speak."
"Leaders need to deliver," Kiran said quietly.
Joseph arrived, grinning, and announced a "bold vision". Anjali nodded along. Two weeks later the draft was missing, Joseph was "still ideating", and Hemlata stayed up finishing it alone.

qa.q: Who did all the data work for Joseph's group last semester?
qa.a: Hemlata did all their data work, on time.

qa.q: Why does Anjali feel Joseph is the obvious leader?
qa.a: His confident, polished way of talking matches her picture of someone who runs things, so it feels like proof of ability even though his record says otherwise.

qa.q: What went wrong in choosing the leader, and what could fix it?
qa.a: They picked the best talker instead of checking who had delivered before; next time the group could look at past work and deadlines, which would point to Hemlata.

qa.q: What is it like for Hemlata to finish the draft alone?
qa.a: Hemlata carries the real work while the title went to someone else, which is likely tiring and feels unfair.

grounding: Shows a student assuming the fluent, confident speaker will run the project well while overlooking the quieter teammate who delivers.

passage: Last year I chose the wrong head for our college fest committee, and I still think about why. I'm Chandrika, the one who ran the vote. Amandeep gave a speech that made the whole room clap: big sponsors, a famous DJ, "the best fest this city has seen." Sonam, who had quietly handled permissions and budgets for two years, said only, "I'll make sure it runs on time." I remember thinking Sonam sounded small. Amandeep sounded like a leader. So I pushed the committee his way. Three weeks before the fest, no sponsor had signed and the stage booking had lapsed. Sonam fixed most of it in ten days. I'd mistaken a good speech for a good plan.

qa.q: What did Sonam say during the speeches?
qa.a: Sonam said only, "I'll make sure it runs on time."

qa.q: Why did Chandrika push the committee toward Amandeep?
qa.a: Amandeep's speech drew claps and sounded like a leader, while Sonam's plain line sounded small, so style felt like proof of competence.

qa.q: What could Chandrika do differently when choosing a head next time?
qa.a: Chandrika could ask each candidate about past work, like permissions and budgets handled, and weigh that record above how impressive a speech sounds.

qa.q: How might Sonam have felt stepping in three weeks before the fest?
qa.a: Sonam may have felt frustrated at being passed over but responsible toward the fest, which is why the fixing still got done.

grounding: Shows a student backing the confident speaker as fest head and overlooking the quieter, more reliable teammate.

passage:
Faculty mentor's note, semester project review. Prof. Pallavi Rao.
Observation: When the second-year design group chose its project lead, Himani argued strongly for Devraj, who presents fluently and confidently. She described Farzana, who speaks little, as "not leadership material." Yet Farzana's lab logs were the only complete ones in the group, and her prototype was the one that worked in the demo. Under Devraj, two deadlines slipped. When I asked Himani what she had based her choice on, she said, "He just seemed like he'd know what to do."
Action taken: I asked the group to review each member's actual contributions from the logs, and suggested they rotate the lead for the next phase. Himani agreed to propose Farzana.

qa.q: Whose lab logs were the only complete ones?
qa.a: Farzana's lab logs were the only complete ones in the group.

qa.q: What does Himani's answer, "He just seemed like he'd know what to do," reveal about her thinking?
qa.a: It shows she judged by how confident and fluent Devraj sounded, not by any record, so his style felt like competence to her.

qa.q: How did Prof. Pallavi Rao help the group correct the choice?
qa.a: The mentor asked them to review each member's real contributions in the logs and to rotate the lead, which puts evidence above impressions.

qa.q: How might Farzana see being called "not leadership material"?
qa.a: Farzana may feel overlooked and discouraged, since her complete logs and working prototype were not counted as leadership.

grounding: Shows a student choosing a fluent, confident teammate as lead and overlooking the quieter one whose work was more reliable.

passage:
Saturday, 2 a.m., hackathon, day 2
I picked the wrong team lead and I know it now.
Yesterday at the kickoff, Pankaj gave this amazing pitch: hands moving, jokes, words like "scalable" and "user journey." Everyone clapped. I thought, obviously he's leading, he sounds like someone who runs a startup. Salma, who sits next to me in the lab, said almost nothing. She just asked two quiet questions about the database. I didn't even think of her.
Now it's 2 a.m. Pankaj has been "networking" at the snack table for three hours. Salma has built the whole backend, fixed my login bug, and quietly written a task list on the whiteboard that everyone is following.
I think I confused sounding good with being good. I'm Hrithik, 20, supposedly smart, and I fell for a speech.
Tomorrow I'll suggest Salma presents the demo too.

qa.q: What has Salma built by 2 a.m.?
qa.a: She has built the whole backend.

qa.q: Why did it feel obvious to Hrithik that Pankaj should lead?
qa.a: Pankaj's confident pitch, with jokes and startup words, matched Hrithik's picture of a leader, so the style felt like proof of skill.

qa.q: What choice does Hrithik make for tomorrow, and why is it fair?
qa.a: Hrithik will suggest Salma presents the demo too, giving credit and visibility to the teammate whose work is actually holding the project together.

qa.q: How might Salma feel if she is asked to present the demo?
qa.a: She may be nervous about speaking up but pleased that her quiet, steady work has finally been noticed.

grounding: A student at a hackathon realises the team lead was chosen for a fluent, confident pitch while a quiet, more reliable teammate was overlooked.

passage:
Samir: bro who should direct the street play for the college fest?
Francis: hmm
Samir: i'm saying Rustam. did you hear him at the meeting? so confident, total director energy 🎬
Francis: he did talk a lot
Samir: exactly. Leela barely said a word
Francis: Leela directed the one-act last year. the one that won
Francis: she's the one who booked the hall, made the rehearsal chart and got the permissions
Samir: ya but she's so quiet. can she handle 20 people?
Francis: she handled 15 last year?? 😅
Francis: rustam missed 3 of 5 rehearsals for the orientation skit
Samir: ...ok i didn't know that
Samir: i think i just liked how he sounded
Francis: happens. ask them both for a plan by friday and compare?
Samir: fair. doing that

qa.q: How many rehearsals did Rustam miss for the orientation skit?
qa.a: Rustam missed 3 of 5 rehearsals for the orientation skit.

qa.q: Why was Samir drawn to Rustam as director?
qa.a: Rustam spoke confidently at the meeting and seemed to have "director energy," which fit Samir's idea of a leader. Leela's quietness made her seem less able, even without evidence.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the chat, and what does Samir decide to do?
qa.a: When Francis listed Leela's record and Rustam's missed rehearsals, Samir admitted to just liking how Rustam sounded. Samir decides to ask both for a plan by Friday and compare.

qa.q: If you were Leela, how might you feel about being passed over for being quiet?
qa.a: You might feel frustrated and invisible, since you already proved you could direct and organise, and you'd hope people looked at your work.

grounding: A student almost chooses a confident talker to direct a play and overlooks a quiet teammate with a strong record, until a friend points it out.
